transcript.text:
Greyhollow clings to the flank of Mount Anvi like a creature sheltering in the stone itself: houses cut into the rock, chimneys venting through the cliff, the whole town stitched downward toward the mine gates. Cold comes off the mountain in waves, and even at this hour the light of late afternoon is already going grey. You are Brakka Ironvein, a dwarf of the Anvil Father, six years a guard at His temple — and you know these workings the way a man knows the shape of his own door.

Three days ago three miners went into the old north workings, sealed a generation back, and did not return. Last night a fourth man clawed his way up alone, whispering of lights that walk, and was dead by dawn. At sunrise the council means to brick the entrance shut, missing men and all. The prior, Hessa, asked you to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. No one else would.

Now you stand at the mine mouth. The borrowed temple lantern hangs from your fist, its little flame licking the glass, and before you the tunnel drops into darkness, the old timbers sagging, the air smelling of stone-dust and something else — a faint, cold breath rising from below. Behind you the town shrinks into evening quiet.

What do you do?

I check the lantern's oil and tug my shield strap tight, then crouch at the tunnel mouth to look for fresh tracks in the dust, boot prints or drag marks from the three miners or the fourth man. If the trail is clear, I'll follow it down slowly, keeping the lantern low and listening for anything walking below.

You loosen the lantern's cap and check the oil — more than half full, the wick trimmed, enough for a long burn. The shield strap is sound; you tug it tight on your arm and ease the longsword a hand's breadth from its scabbard before letting it fall back.

Crouched at the tunnel mouth, you study the dust. The floor is thick with it, grey and fine, untouched for a generation except where the seal was broken. There are prints — but the soft dust has settled and blurred them, and the fourth man's passage last night has churned the middle of the floor into a smeared, dragging path. You can make out the general way of it: one frantic, stumbling track coming up, and beneath it the older imprints of several heavier feet going down. Which belong to the three miners and which to the man who died, you can't be sure anymore. The trail down is clear enough to follow, anyway.

You step inside. The lantern's flame steadies as you lower it, and the tunnel walls come up gold out of the black — old timber, sagging but whole, the rock sweating cold. The floor runs gently downward. Your steps and the soft creak of the shoring are very loud in the hush, and beneath the smell of dust there is that same cold, faint breath rising, moving as if the mountain were exhaling. You go slow, listening.

The tunnel runs a fair way on a straight, gentle grade, then opens out. You stand on a high ledge where the passage widens into a great worked chamber, its far wall lost in gloom. To your left a crude barricade of rotted planks lies half toppled — the old seal, broken through from the far side. Then the floor of the chamber drops away into darkness, and you cannot yet say how deep, or what is below.

What do you do?

I stop at the ledge and keep the lantern low and shuttered a bit so I don't blind myself to the dark below. I examine the toppled barricade first: which way were the planks pushed, and is there anything like scratches, blood, or dropped gear on it? Then I pick up a loose stone and drop it over the edge, listening for how far it falls.

A natural 20 — under the house rule, this succeeds beyond a plain success, with a discovery that matters. Let me examine the barricade closely.

You thumb the lantern's shutter half closed, so the light pools at your feet and your eyes can find the true dark below. Then you set to the barricade.

The planks are rotted almost to sponge, and the story is plain once you look close. The old seal was broken through from the far side — out, toward the entry tunnel you came down. The splintered ends lean inward, and the iron pins that once held the timbers are bent back the same way, the wood torn off them from within. It was pushed down, not stepped on; a miner's boot would have crushed the boards flat and left them lying outward, but instead they stand peeled and leaning against the rock.

And there is more. The stone around those pins is chipped in close, ordered rows — not the ragged ring of a pick, but hundreds of shallow, patient little scrapes, as though something with fingers had worked at the stone for a long time, from the far side, before the seal ever went up. On the planks themselves you find old scratches and the yellow-brown curl of a torn-off fingernail, long desiccated. Whoever, or whatever, tried the seal long ago had hands.

No blood of the three miners, nor of the fourth man, lies on the barricade. Whatever came through it last night did not bleed on the way.

You straighten, take up a loose chunk of stone, and let it fall over the ledge. It clicks once off rock, and then the silence drinks it. You count. Three seconds before the echo of its landing comes up, faint and far. A long, long drop — forty yards and more, and the bottom ringing like a floor cut from living stone.

What do you do?

I look along the chamber walls near the ledge for a path down, like a stair, ramp, ladder, or old mining scaffold. If I find a safe way, I'll start descending slowly with the lantern low, but if not I'll consider the rope in my pack.

RULE Vision and Light:
The most fundamental tasks of adventuring--noticing danger, finding hidden objects, hitting an enemy in combat, and targeting a spell, to name just a few--rely heavily on a character's ability to see. Darkness and other effects that obscure vision can prove a significant hindrance.

A given area might be lightly or heavily obscured. In a **lightly obscured** area, such as dim light, patchy fog, or moderate foliage, creatures have disadvantage on Wisdom (Perception) checks that rely on sight.

A **heavily obscured** area-such as darkness, opaque fog, or dense foliage-blocks vision entirely. A creature effectively suffers from the blinded condition (see appendix PH-A) when trying to see something in that area.

The presence or absence of light in an environment creates three categories of illumination: bright light, dim light, and darkness.

**Bright light** lets most creatures see normally.

Even gloomy days provide bright light, as do torches, lanterns, fires, and other sources of illumination within a specific radius.

**Dim light**, also called shadows, creates a lightly obscured area. An area of dim light is usually a boundary between a source of bright light, such as a torch, and surrounding darkness. The soft light of twilight and dawn also counts as dim light. A particularly brilliant full moon might bathe the land in dim light.

**Darkness** creates a heavily obscured area.

Characters face darkness outdoors at night (even most moonlit nights), within the confines of an unlit dungeon or a subterranean vault, or in an area of magical darkness.

#### Blindsight

A creature with blindsight can perceive its surroundings without relying on sight, within a specific radius. Creatures without eyes, such as oozes, and creatures with echolocation or heightened senses, such as bats and true dragons, have this sense.

#### Darkvision

Many creatures in fantasy gaming worlds, especially those that dwell underground, have darkvision. Within a specified range, a creature with darkvision can see in darkness as if the darkness were dim light, so areas of darkness are only lightly obscured as far as that creature is concerned. However, the creature can't discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.

#### Truesight

A creature with truesight can, out to a specific range, see in normal and magical darkness, see invisible creatures and objects, automatically detect visual illusions and succeed on saving throws against them, and perceives the original form of a shapechanger or a creature that is transformed by magic. Furthermore, the creature can see into the Ethereal Plane.

Ordered, patient scraping on the stone around the old barricade's iron pins, made by something like fingers rather than picks, before the seal was put up a generation ago — on the far side of the seal.

A long, pale groove worn up the center of the chamber stair steps, and rougher scraped stone on the walls, as if something with claws climbed or descended the old stair many times. The groove is old, smooth at its edges, not fresh — not made in the last few days. The claw-spacing suggests three or four toes to each limb, like a dog's paw but larger.

In the thin rock-dust on the chamber floor at the foot of the stair, boot tracks show several miners going down and one set coming back up. Three men went deeper into the chamber, their prints pressed deep and orderly, and a fourth, lighter-shod, staggered and fell more than once. The miners' gear — a dropped pick and a tin cup — lies scattered where the tracks begin.

A miner's pick dropped and left near the stair-foot of the great chamber. Clean — no blood — but the haft bears an owner's mark scratched deep: a crude A over an anvil, and the letters 'K. H.' scratched below it.
A dented tin miner's cup, dropped near the stair-foot of the great chamber. Clean, no blood.
A miner whose pick, marked 'K. H.', was dropped in the old north workings. Likely one of the three lost miners.

On the chamber floor, a wide shallow ring of scattered coins (copper, silver, a few gold) and a pair of miner's boots left sole-down in a line, as if the three miners walked out of their own boots and emptied their pockets as they went. No blood, no bodies. Beyond the boots the tracks continue as bare footprints, not dragged — the men kept walking deeper barefoot and lighter.

sheet.name: Brakka Ironvein
sheet.opening: Brakka Ironvein served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside. Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, which were sealed a generation ago, and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up out of the dark alone, babbling about lights that walk, then died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. The temple's prior, an old dwarf named Hessa, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. It is late afternoon, and Brakka stands at the mine mouth with a lantern borrowed from the temple.

input.text:
Greyhollow clings to the flank of Mount Anvi like a creature sheltering in the stone itself: houses cut into the rock, chimneys venting through the cliff, the whole town stitched downward toward the mine gates. Cold comes off the mountain in waves, and even at this hour the light of late afternoon is already going grey. You are Brakka Ironvein, a dwarf of the Anvil Father, six years a guard at His temple — and you know these workings the way a man knows the shape of his own door.

Three days ago three miners went into the old north workings, sealed a generation back, and did not return. Last night a fourth man clawed his way up alone, whispering of lights that walk, and was dead by dawn. At sunrise the council means to brick the entrance shut, missing men and all. You thumb the lantern's shutter half closed, so the light pools at your feet and your eyes can find the true dark below. Then you set to the barricade.

The planks are rotted almost to sponge, and the story is plain once you look close. The old seal was broken through from the far side — out, toward the entry tunnel you came down. The splintered ends lean inward, and the iron pins that once held the timbers are bent back the same way, the wood torn off them from within. It was pushed down, not stepped on; a miner's boot would have crushed the boards flat and left them lying outward, but instead they stand peeled and leaning against the rock.

And there is more. The stone around those pins is chipped in close, ordered rows — not the ragged ring of a pick, but hundreds of shallow, patient little scrapes, as though something with fingers had worked at the stone for a long time, from the far side, before the seal ever went up. On the planks themselves you find old scratches and the yellow-brown curl of a torn-off fingernail, long desiccated. Whoever, or whatever, tried the seal long ago had hands.

No blood of the three miners, nor of the fourth man, lies on the barricade. Whatever came through it last night did not bleed on the way.

You straighten, take up a loose chunk of stone, and let it fall over the ledge. It clicks once off rock, and then the silence drinks it. You count. Three seconds before the echo of its landing comes up, faint and far. A long, long drop — forty yards and more, and the bottom ringing like a floor cut from living stone.

The most fundamental tasks of adventuring--noticing danger, finding hidden objects, hitting an enemy in combat, and targeting a spell, to name just a few--rely heavily on a character's ability to see. Darkness and other effects that obscure vision can prove a significant hindrance.

The presence or absence of light in an environment creates three categories of illumination: bright light, dim light, and darkness.

**Dim light**, also called shadows, creates a lightly obscured area. An area of dim light is usually a boundary between a source of bright light, such as a torch, and surrounding darkness.
